analysis.one_liner: Requires notice, review, and proof before removing voters from registration rolls, and bars registration denials over database mismatches.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Administration Committee: introduced October 15, 2009 with zero cosponsors, it received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended federal voting law to make it harder to remove registered voters from the rolls by mistake. It would require states to mail a notice at least 30 days before removing anyone for a reason other than death or moving, give the voter a way to challenge the removal, and let the voter cast a provisional ballot that gets counted if the removal turns out to be wrong. If a voter challenged the removal, the state would have to prove by clear and convincing evidence that it was justified. The bill would also stop states from refusing or delaying registration just because a driver's license or Social Security number failed to match a government database, and require states to accept the completed national registration form. All of it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered voters at risk of being wrongfully struck from the rolls: people who move often, students, naturalized citizens, people whose names are recorded with slight variations, and voters flagged over criminal-conviction or mental-incapacity records that are actually mismatches or outdated. Under the bill, they would get advance notice, a free way to contest removal, a provisional ballot counted if the removal was in error, and a rule that the state must prove a challenged removal was proper.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters vulnerable to wrongful roll purges

how_it_helps.text: States would have to send forwardable mail at least 30 days before any removal for a reason other than death or moving, stating the reason and how to contest it, with a prepaid return envelope [S3].
A challenged removal could not take effect unless the election official demonstrates by clear and convincing evidence that the voter was properly removed [S3].
A voter who receives a removal notice could cast a provisional ballot, and it would be counted if the removal decision was made in error [S3].

States could not refuse or delay a registration solely because the applicant's driver's license or Social Security information failed to match state motor vehicle, Social Security, or other government databases [S3].

States could not reject an applicant who completed all information required on the national voter registration form, and could not require extra citizenship or age documents beyond the signed penalty-of-perjury attestation [S3].

Removals for moving would require verification by matching the voter's name, date of birth, and identifying number against the registration in the new jurisdiction, rather than relying on a returned mailing alone [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local election offices would bear the cost of mailing notices before purges, running review processes within 10 days of a challenge, and matching records across jurisdictions, and they would carry the burden of proving challenged removals were proper. Politicians and party operatives who rely on aggressive list-maintenance to remove marginal voters would lose a tool.
analysis.who_pays_short: State election offices and purge practitioners

drawbacks.text: Requiring clear and convincing evidence before a challenged removal takes effect could make it harder for states to remove voters who are genuinely ineligible, such as people registered in two jurisdictions or those with a disqualifying conviction, and could slow legitimate list maintenance [S3].

Barring registration denial solely on a database mismatch means a state could not use a failed driver's license or Social Security check to stop a registration, which opponents of such rules argued weakened a safeguard against non-citizen or duplicate registrations; the bill relies on the signed penalty-of-perjury attestation instead [S3].
Pre-election notice, prepaid mailings, and 10-day review deadlines would impose new administrative burdens and costs on state and county election offices, including small ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real, documented problem: eligible voters struck from the rolls over database mismatches, stale records, or mistaken criminal and mental-incapacity flags, often without notice until they show up to vote. The protections are strongly weighted toward keeping voters on the rolls, and the burden-shifting to the state is the bill's most aggressive feature; honest critics would say it complicates removing voters who are truly ineligible. The mandatory audit guidance was only voluntary. On balance it traded some ease of list maintenance for a much lower risk of wrongfully disenfranchising registered voters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rush Holt of New Jersey introduced the bill on October 15, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration [S1] [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials and others who benefit from rapid, low-verification voter list removal faced no new federal notice, review, or proof requirements, and election administrators avoided the bill's mailing, matching, and review workload. The voters the bill was written to protect got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials free to purge without new checks

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Protection Against Wrongful Voter Purges Act on October 15, 2009.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its October 15, 2009 referral and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Members
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors during the bill's lifetime.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is recorded, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; the only recorded facts are a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of any party [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Political parties and groups that rely on aggressive voter-list purging
industries.note: The bill died, so no new notice, review, or proof requirements constrain removal of marginal voters from the rolls. Groups whose electoral prospects improve when infrequent or mismatched voters are removed keep the status quo.

Had it passed, election offices would have shouldered new notice, matching, and 10-day review duties and a heightened burden of proof for contested removals. Its death spared them that workload while leaving their list-maintenance practices unchanged.
